> Electrotrack is a multi-stage electromagnetic ball accelerator (coilgun) with a custom PCB. An ESP32 reads IR photo-interrupters along a 3D-printed track and fires a sequence of coils to pull a steel ball forward. Each coil is switched off as the ball reaches its center, so it isn't pulled back. Hardware - ESP32 controller, 4 coil channels (logic-level N-MOSFETs + flyback diodes) - Coils wound from 0.3 mm copper wire - 3S LiPo (≈12 V)  - IR position sensors salvaged from a photocopier - 7.5 mm steel ball *Inspired by Hyperspace Pirate's electromagnetic accelerator project.*

### Day 1 (05.10, 4:00pm–9:00pm): Ideas, decisions and schematic

**How it started**  
I watched Hyperspace Pirate's video *"Electromagnetic Accelerator Improvements Part II"* and realized that building something similar was well within reach. That's when I decided to make it my Half-Life project, featuring a custom PCB to control the system.

> *Inspiration: Hyperspace Pirate's Electromagnetic Accelerator project*  
![inspiration](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/229890c17214dee5c3dc695fed51462b1cc270b4c3bc81aaf889bd493b4f221c.jpg)

**Design decisions**

- **Power:** 3S LiPo battery (already on hand).
- **Coils:** Wound from 0.3 mm copper wire (plenty available). Planning 4 coils for the initial setup.

> *Coils match-cut*  
![coils](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/71cedc5ea22cd10fc80464ccd9d67abb825a0e5668672fb1b5a6fdf055d60a76.gif)

> *0.3 mm copper wire spool and 3S LiPo battery*  
![wire and battery](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/1b4818696516cfcd65c9d9b305f46254e9cbe6af19df525b42753f2ee66ec82e.jpeg)

- **Projectile:** Found two steel balls (7.5 mm and 12 mm). Testing both to determine the optimal choice.

> *Candidate projectiles: 7.5 mm and 12 mm steel balls*  
![Projectile](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/af06d2e8b73eb9ff7e527acea8892c0e2878ffcb147529d9b1676d1299a14ed2.jpeg)

- **Mechanics:** 3D-printed guide track and structure.
- **Controller:** ESP32 microcontroller instead of a purely analog timing circuit. It provides precise timing control and allows dedicated firmware development.

> *ESP32 microcontroller board match-cut*  
![esp32](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/d5ed859be637f06426b84676c2a9aaf4206ab331de815162c584bc8f38bfe8fc.gif)

- **Sensors:** Salvaged IR photo-interrupters from an old photocopier, eliminating the need to purchase new sensors.

> *IR sensors match-cut*  
![IR](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/068eac135437a217ea9e9b019de667c8a639f1ed608a0acf771ed3847d246c86.gif)

> *Close-up of the salvaged IR sensor components*  
![IR sens](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/f0be89724ac1c92f1d7a64a0cabe4008d0fbb140a3ac6a409150d595b01b1ff4.jpeg)

**Schematic**  
I carefully drew the complete circuit by hand on paper (~3 hours including research): featuring an ESP32, 4 MOSFET channels, coil drivers with flyback diodes, IR position sensors, and power regulation (12 V input to L7805 5 V regulator feeding the ESP32 VIN). The rest of the afternoon was spent refining decisions and recording footage for the video reel.

> *Drafting the circuit schematic by hand*  
![drawing](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/6afd34f153f555bcad915ce59f7bc9067bcb158de39e4ea21b4971c7ef149735.gif)

> *Completed hand-drawn schematic diagram*  
![schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/f7ba8cd80ad2b3ba156fc6c0146ebd6b72a234233b0c6e983505987c3b2d455c.jpeg)

**Problems & Solutions**

- **Bare IR sensors:** They consist only of raw IR LEDs and phototransistors. Added 220 Ω current-limiting resistors for LEDs and 10 kΩ external pull-up resistors for phototransistors, as ESP32 input-only pins lack internal pull-ups.
- **Powering ESP32 from 12 V:** Lacking a buck converter, I utilized an L7805 linear regulator. Heat dissipation will be managed with a small heatsink.
- **ESP32 pin selection:** Avoided strapping pins during boot and mapped all IR sensor inputs to dedicated input-only pins (GPIs).

### 2026-10-11: Week 1 – Entry 2: KiCad schematic, PCB layout and routing

**11.68h**

Week 1 – Entry 2: KiCad schematic, PCB layout and routing
Total time: ~7.2 h (recorded in timelapses)

* ~3 h: KiCad schematic, footprints and BOM
* ~2 h: component placement + OLED and spare-GPIO headers
* ~1 h: routing the 2-layer board
* ~1 h: DRC fixes, Gerber/BOM export and GitHub repo
* ~1 h: editing the timelapse reel & writing Entry 2

Day 3 (07.10): KiCad schematic, footprints and BOM
I redrew the hand-drawn schematic in KiCad: ESP32 30-pin devkit, 4 coil channels (IRLZ44N MOSFET, 100 ohm gate resistor, 10k pull-down, SB560 flyback diode), 4 IR sensor inputs (JST XH connectors with resistors), 12 V input through an XT30 connector with fuse and switch, and an L7805 for 5 V.

![schematic](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/3b39a14ae5428734f6d433e6eb5703f1005094a694422dabb4213581d63f6829.png)

KiCad schematic

Then I assigned footprints and exported the BOM.

![footprint](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/3065b54ca51a5a8df67fa0073e07a85f3dae258c72068315989d50682df1c4ff.png)

Footprints assigned and loaded into the PCB editor

Day 4 (08.10): Component placement
I placed all components on the board, then added two extras: a 0.96" I2C OLED header (SDA on GPIO21, SCL on GPIO22) to show ball speed, and a 1x10 header with spare GPIOs, 3.3 V and GND for future needs.

Day 5 (10.10): Tidying the layout
I regrouped the parts: each coil channel in one row (terminal, flyback diode, MOSFET, resistors), power input and capacitors in one corner, ESP32 with the USB port at the board edge, and IR connectors on the opposite side.

Day 6 (11.10): Routing, DRC and fabrication files
I routed a 2-layer board: 2.5 mm traces for 12 V, 1.5-2.5 mm for coil nets, 0.3-0.5 mm for signals, and a GND copper pour on both layers. Then I ran DRC and fixed all errors (thermal relief errors solved with solid pad connections, plus one unconnected GND pad). Only silkscreen warnings are left. Finally I exported Gerbers, drill files, BOM and schematic, and pushed everything to GitHub.

![3d](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/86fe5185d5067398fa694d7c6ad49d3f62786b66d3601bcc5b141c53852f79a0.png)

3D view of the finished PCB

Problems & Solutions

* Wrong layer count: the imported JLCPCB template had 4 copper layers. I switched the board to 2 layers in Board Setup.
* XT30 polarity: the + and - were swapped between my schematic and the footprint. I fixed it in the schematic before routing.
* MOSFET gate drive: the IRLZ44N gate is driven from 3.3 V, but the datasheet specifies its on-resistance only for 4-5 V. I decided to keep it for this version and measure the drain-source voltage when I build it. A gate driver can be added later if needed.
* DRC errors: the GND pour used a 0.5 mm clearance and thermal reliefs, which left some pads under-connected. Changing it to a 0.3 mm clearance and solid pad connections fixed all errors.
* Gate and pull-down resistors (open item from Entry 1): chose 100 ohm gate resistors and 10k pull-downs, so the MOSFETs stay off while the ESP32 boots.
* IR LED resistors: the schematic uses 150 ohm from 3.3 V (about 14 mA, assuming about 1.2 V forward voltage) instead of the 220 ohm I first planned. I will verify this with the real sensors.

Still to check / Next steps

* Measure the coil DC resistance and check that the 5 A fuse matches the peak current.
* Measure the MOSFET drain-source voltage with a 3.3 V gate drive during a coil pulse.
* Check how hot the L7805 gets.
* Firmware must limit the on-time of each coil.
* Order the PCB and parts after approval, wind the coils and 3D-print the track.

Additional hours (not covered by the timelapses)
The extra hours I added to this entry (~2 h in total) come from work that is not on the timelapses:

CHANGES MADE AFTER REVIEW (resubmission)
The project was reviewed and returned with "Design needs changes". Everything in this section was done AFTER that review, in response to the reviewer's feedback.

Reviewer feedback:
1. Make the README more descriptive: what the project is, what it does / what its purpose is, and why it exists.
2. Start writing the firmware now.

Time spent on these changes: ~2.5 h (~1.5 h README, ~1 h firmware), not covered by the timelapses.

1) README: more descriptive (~1 h)
* Added sections explaining what Electrotrack is, what it is intended to do and why I am building it (inspired by Hyperspace Pirate's videos, and a way to learn the full path from schematic to PCB, CAD, firmware and prototype).
* Added a hardware overview, a project files table, a status checklist and ESP32 connections
* Added a Firmware section to the README (see below).

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/8a4c31281db1a7519e1cf9cab3b343352e3352b508aeff322f3db49ccf151ec8.png)
2) Firmware: first draft (~1 h)
The firmware is in the repo at software/firmware/firmware.ino and is described in the "Firmware" section of the README. It was written with AI assistance (vibe coding), and the README says so clearly. It has not been tested on hardware yet.
* An IR sensor sits just before each coil. When the ball is detected, an interrupt switches that coil on and schedules the switch-off for when the ball reaches the coil centre, based on the speed measured between the previous two sensors.
* A high-priority task waits for the switch-off time with microsecond precision, so the timing does not depend on the 1 ms FreeRTOS tick.
* Software safety: 80 ms maximum on-time per coil, the previous coil is forced off when the next sensor fires, a run stops after 400 sensor events, and any fault switches all coils off until the next start.
* The OLED shows the current speed, peak speed and hit count. BOOT starts and stops a run.
* The code has a setting IR_TRIGGER EDGE) that lets it be tried in an online simulator with push buttons instead of the IR sensors.
* After writing the draft I reviewed it against the schematic and fixed two problems: the IR pin order in the code was outdated (now 36, 35, 34, 39 for J1-J4), and the coil timeout check in loop() could report a false fault because of a timing race with the interrupt. I also tidied the code.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/D1H5wjMaoqfsZfeTslugwWB4nIQcEzNR/c0592f5683bc9674452e3192d88c9f875cb72fc87f840fddcecb5d45524df252.png)

Next steps for the firmware: test it on the real board, tune the switch-off timing and update the geometry values (sensor spacing, sensor-to-coil-centre distance)

### 2026-11-26: Today before school I started testing the IR sensors. I used AI to write the test code, it has a browser dashboard for showing the sonsor data and also shows it on the OLED display on the PCB. I solde

**4h**

Today before school I started testing the IR sensors. I used AI to write the test code, it has a browser dashboard for showing the sonsor data and also shows it on the OLED display on the PCB. I soldered one sensor but the display was showing incorrect data. It turned out that it was just the pins of the sensors were assigned wrong. After I  fixed this it worked well. when the WIFI on the esp32 was turned on and I was powering it from my bench supply at 9V the current was ~0,150A. I checked how hot was the 5V regulator getting, it was getting quite warm, but not hot so for now I am not adding any heatsink. Without vibe coding before school I spend around 1h on this project.

After school I vibe coded the rest of the code it has the sensor test dashboard with the interrupt-driven coil controler, speed calculation, and coil timeout safety logic

Then I printed the coil bobbin, sensor module and two track praats from grey PETG. Wound the coil using 0.3mm copper wire I made six layers of copper wire on in the bobbin it took me very long (~1.5) because I didn'd have expierience winding and also I wanted to do it perfectly, it did'd turn out like this but I think it's pretty good. then I soldered the sensor and started testing. I tried to get that one coil and a sensor to accelerate the ball through that part of a track using slightly modified firmwere but I did'd manage to do that. After that I tried to light up an LED using the sensor and the coil input after even that didn'd work I just rage quited for that day.
